Econometrics

A complete reading on econometrics: from probability and statistics through the algebra, geometry, finite-sample and large-sample theory of ordinary least squares (OLS), to endogeneity, instrumental variables and GMM, maximum likelihood and discrete choice, panel data, counterfactuals and treatment effects (LATE, regression discontinuity, matching, propensity scores), and finally a short introduction to Bayesian methods. Textbooks often cut this material into a string of unconnected "tests" and "estimators". This text takes a different view: all of econometrics is one story unfolding —

first define the object we care about in the population (conditional expectation, linear projection, causal effect) → build an estimator by the analogy principle (replace population moments with sample moments) → prove it consistent with the law of large numbers → derive its distribution with the central limit theorem → do tests and confidence intervals → when assumptions fail (endogeneity, selection, clustering) redesign the estimator.

Each chapter first says what question it answers and what the intuition is, then gives definitions, results and proof ideas, and finally works the simplest example.

Prerequisites: linear algebra (matrices, projections), probability (expectation, variance, conditional expectation), a little calculus.

Notation

  • y is the dependent variable, x (k\times1) the regressors, e or u the error; the sample (y_i,x_i)_{i=1}^n is stacked into y\;(n\times1) and X\;(n\times k).
  • \iota is the vector of ones; P_X=X(X'X)^{-1}X' the projection matrix and M_X=I-P_X the residual-maker.
  • \to^p is convergence in probability, \to^d convergence in distribution; \operatorname{plim} the probability limit.
  • \operatorname{Var}(\cdot|X) is a conditional variance; \operatorname{AVar} an asymptotic variance.
  • Q_{xx}=E[x_ix_i'], \Omega=E[x_ix_i'e_i^2].

0. The Big Picture: What Does Econometrics Do?

0.1 One question, three layers of answers

Intuition. Suppose you want to know "by how much does one more year of schooling raise wages on average?" There is a definite number \beta in the population, but you have only a random sample. Econometrics answers three nested questions:

  1. Estimation: what is the best guess \hat\beta of \beta from the sample? (OLS, MLE, GMM)
  2. Inference: how reliable is that guess? How large is the error? Is a hypothesis true? (standard errors, t/F tests, confidence intervals)
  3. Identification: even with infinite data, does \beta equal the causal effect we want? (endogeneity, instruments, randomisation, discontinuities)

The third is the deepest: statistical consistency is not causal interpretation. OLS consistently estimates a "linear projection", which need not be a causal effect — the motivation for the whole second half (endogeneity, panels, treatment effects).

0.2 The thread: the analogy principle + large samples

Nearly every estimator comes from one recipe:

  1. the population satisfies a moment condition E[m(w_i,\theta_0)]=0 (OLS: E[x_i(y_i-x_i'\beta)]=0; IV: E[z_i(y_i-x_i'\beta)]=0; MLE: the expected score is zero);
  2. analogy principle: replace the expectation with a sample average, \frac1n\sum m(w_i,\hat\theta)=0;
  3. LLN ⟹ consistency; CLT + delta method ⟹ asymptotic normality with a "sandwich" variance A^{-1}BA^{-1}.

1. Probability and Statistics Foundations

Intuition. This chapter is a toolbox: only concepts used again and again later, with intuition. Expectation is a "weighted average"; conditional expectation is "the best prediction given information"; the law of large numbers says a sample mean converges to the population mean; the central limit theorem says the error of that convergence is normal.

1.1 Probability spaces and random variables

  • A probability space (\Omega,\mathcal F,P): sample space, \sigma-algebra of events, probability measure. Basics: P(\emptyset)=0, P(A^c)=1-P(A).
  • Independence P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B); conditional probability P(A|B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B); total probability P(A)=\sum_iP(A\cap B_i); Bayes' rule P(B|A)=\dfrac{P(A|B)P(B)}{P(A)}.
  • A random variable X:\Omega\to\mathbb R; CDF F_X(a)=P(X\le a); PDF f_X=F_X'; conditional density f(y|x)=f(x,y)/f(x).
  • Transformations: if Y=G(X) with G monotone, f_Y(y)=\big|\tfrac{d}{dy}G^{-1}(y)\big|f_X(G^{-1}(y)); in several dimensions multiply by the Jacobian determinant.
  • Moments: E[X^r]; variance \operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2; covariance \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y].
  • Law of iterated expectations: E[E[Y|X]]=E[Y]; E[E[Y|X_1,X_2]|X_1]=E[Y|X_1].
  • Hazard rate: H(x)=\dfrac{f_X(x)}{1-F_X(x)}.

Inequalities: Chebyshev P(g(X)\ge r)\le E[g(X)]/r; Jensen (E[g(X)]\ge g(E[X]) for convex g); Hölder E|XY|\le(E|X|^p)^{1/p}(E|Y|^q)^{1/q} (\frac1p+\frac1q=1); Minkowski.

1.2 Linear projection

Intuition. The conditional expectation E[y|x] is the best prediction of y, but it can be complicated. The linear projection is the best prediction among linear functions.

Definition. P(y|x)=x'\beta with

\beta=E[xx']^{-1}E[xy]=\arg\min_bE[(y-x'b)^2].
First-order condition E[x(y-x'\beta)]=0: the residual is uncorrelated with x. Properties: linearity; the law of iterated projections P(P(y|x_1,x_2)|x_1)=P(y|x_1).

1.4 Sampling and convergence

  • A random sample X_1,\dots,X_n is iid; an estimator is a function of the sample \hat\theta=T(X_1,\dots,X_n); its distribution is the sampling distribution.
  • Convergence in probability X_n\to^pc: P(|X_n-c|<\epsilon)\to1; in distribution X_n\to^dX: CDFs converge pointwise. Orders: X_n=O_p(n^r) means X_n/n^r is bounded in probability; o_p(n^r) means X_n/n^r\to^p0.
  • Continuous mapping theorem: if X_n\to^p\mu_X, Y_n\to^p\mu_Y, Z_n\to^dZ, sums, products, quotients (nonzero denominator) and continuous functions preserve convergence, and X_nZ_n\to^d\mu_XZ (Slutsky).

1.5 LLN, CLT and the delta method

  • Weak law of large numbers (LLN): iid, E|X_i|<\infty ⟹ \bar X_n\to^p\mu.
  • Central limit theorem (CLT): iid, \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\Sigma<\infty ⟹ \sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\to^dN(0,\Sigma).
  • Delta method: if \sqrt n(X_n-\mu)\to^dN(0,\Sigma) and g is differentiable at \mu,
    \sqrt n\big(g(X_n)-g(\mu)\big)\to^dN\big(0,\,Dg(\mu)'\Sigma\,Dg(\mu)\big).

Intuition. The LLN tells you where the sample mean goes, the CLT how it gets there: the error is of order 1/\sqrt n and normal. In the figure, even when the underlying distribution is strongly skewed (exponential), the standardised mean of n draws approaches the normal curve quickly.

1.6 Point estimation

  • Maximum likelihood (MLE): L_n(\theta)=\prod f(X_i,\theta), \hat\theta=\arg\max\sum\ln f(X_i,\theta).
  • Method of moments (MoM): the population satisfies E[m(X,\theta)]=0; solve \frac1n\sum m(X_i,\hat\theta)=0.
  • Comparing estimators: unbiased E\hat\theta=\theta; mean squared error \operatorname{MSE}=(E\hat\theta-\theta)^2+\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) (bias² + variance); efficiency: smaller variance; consistency: \hat\theta\to^p\theta.
  • Confidence interval: statistics (L,U) with P(\theta\in(L,U))=1-\alpha.

1.7 Hypothesis testing

  • Null H_0:\theta\in\Theta_0, alternative H_1; Type I error: rejecting a true H_0; Type II error: accepting a false H_0.
  • Decision rule: a rejection region C. Size =P(S_n\in C|\theta_0); p-value: the probability under H_0 of a result at least this extreme; power =P(S_n\in C|\theta\in\Theta_1).
  • Convention: control Type I error strictly (fixed size, e.g. 5%) and, given that, seek high power. An unbiased test rejects more often under the alternative than under the null; a consistent test has power tending to 1 as n\to\infty.

2. The Algebra and Geometry of OLS

Intuition. Least squares is in essence one orthogonal projection: the n-vector y is "projected" onto the k-dimensional plane spanned by the columns of X; the foot is \hat y and the perpendicular remainder is the residual \hat e. All algebraic properties — residuals orthogonal to regressors, R^2, partitioned regression (FWL) — are corollaries of this one picture.

2.1 Model and assumptions

General regression model: y=m(x)+\epsilon, E[\epsilon|x]=0, E[\epsilon^2|x]=\sigma^2(x). Linear regression model: y=x'\beta+\epsilon; sample version y=X\beta+e.

Assumption list (referenced later):

Label Content
A1 Random sampling observations iid
A2 No perfect collinearity X'X invertible
A3′ Zero correlation E[xe]=0
A3 Zero conditional mean $E[e
A4′ Heteroskedasticity $E[e^2
A4 Homoskedasticity $E[e^2
A5 Gaussian errors $e

2.2 Estimators: MLE and least squares

OLS: \hat\beta=\arg\min_b\frac1n(y-Xb)'(y-Xb). The first-order condition X'(y-X\hat\beta)=0 (the normal equations) gives

\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y=\Big(\sum x_ix_i'\Big)^{-1}\sum x_iy_i.

MLE: under A1–A5 the log-likelihood \sum\big[-\tfrac12\ln2\pi-\tfrac12\ln\sigma^2-\frac{(y_i-x_i'\beta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big] is maximised in \beta exactly when the sum of squared residuals is minimised, so MLE = OLS, with \hat\sigma^2_{MLE}=\hat e'\hat e/n.

2.3 Projection matrices and residuals

\hat y=X\hat\beta=P_Xy,\qquad\hat e=M_Xy=M_Xe,\qquad P_X=X(X'X)^{-1}X',\ M_X=I-P_X.

Theorem (properties):

  1. P_X,M_X are symmetric and idempotent; P_XX=X, M_XX=0;
  2. X'\hat e=0, \hat y'\hat e=0 (the residual is orthogonal to regressors and fitted values);
  3. with a constant, \sum\hat e_i=0 and \bar y=\bar{\hat y};
  4. \operatorname{tr}(P_X)=k, \operatorname{tr}(M_X)=n-k (using \operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA));
  5. \hat e'\hat e=e'M_Xe=y'M_Xy; P_\iota=\iota\iota'/n, P_\iota y=\bar y\iota.

Leverage: h_{ii}=x_i'(X'X)^{-1}x_i is the i-th diagonal element of P_X; \sum h_{ii}=k, h_{ii}\in[0,1]. The leave-one-out residual \tilde e_i=y_i-x_i'\hat\beta_{(-i)}=\hat e_i/(1-h_{ii}): the higher the leverage the more the point "pulls" the line and the more care it deserves.

Special cases: constant only \Rightarrow\hat\beta=\bar y; one regressor with intercept \Rightarrow\hat\beta_2=\dfrac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}, \hat\beta_1=\bar y-\bar x\hat\beta_2; rescaling: regressing on XC gives \hat\beta^*=C^{-1}\hat\beta and the same \hat y.

2.4 Partitioned regression (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell)

Intuition. "The effect of X_1 controlling for X_2" = first remove from y and X_1 the part explained by X_2, then regress what remains. This is what "controlling for" really means.

Theorem (FWL). For y=X_1\beta_1+X_2\beta_2+e,

\hat\beta_1=(X_1'M_{X_2}X_1)^{-1}X_1'M_{X_2}y,
i.e. regress the residuals of y on the residuals of X_1 (M_{X_2} is "regress on X_2 and keep the residual").

Proof. Partition the normal equations: X_1'(y-X_1\hat\beta_1-X_2\hat\beta_2)=0, X_2'(\cdots)=0. Solve the second for \hat\beta_2=(X_2'X_2)^{-1}X_2'(y-X_1\hat\beta_1) and substitute into the first to get X_1'M_{X_2}X_1\hat\beta_1=X_1'M_{X_2}y. \square

Special case: with a constant, \hat\beta_2=(X_2'M_\iota X_2)^{-1}X_2'M_\iota y: regress demeaned data (the fitted line passes through (\bar x,\bar y)).

2.5 Goodness of fit

  • SST=(y-\bar y\iota)'(y-\bar y\iota), SSR=(\hat y-\bar y\iota)'(\hat y-\bar y\iota) (regression sum of squares), SSE=\hat e'\hat e.
  • Variance decomposition: SST=SSR+SSE (since \hat e\perp\hat y-\bar y\iota).
  • R^2=SSR/SST=1-SSE/SST=\operatorname{corr}(y,\hat y)^2\in[0,1]; adding any variable never lowers R^2 (the new minimisation problem has an extra degree of freedom).
  • Adjusted R^2: 1-\dfrac{SSE/(n-k)}{SST/(n-1)} (k counts the constant); it penalises superfluous variables.

3. Finite-Sample Theory

Intuition. If the errors are normal, every distribution of OLS is exactly known, with no large-sample approximation. This is the origin of the classical t and F tests. Even without normality, unbiasedness and Gauss–Markov optimality need only the first three assumptions.

3.1 Unbiasedness and variance

Theorem. Under A1–A3:

  1. E[\hat\beta|X]=\beta;
  2. \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta|X)=(X'X)^{-1}X'\Sigma X(X'X)^{-1}, \Sigma=E[ee'|X]=\operatorname{diag}[\sigma^2(x_i)] (the sandwich);
  3. \operatorname{Var}(\hat e|X)=M_X\Sigma M_X'. Under homoskedasticity: 4. \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta|X)=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}; 5. \operatorname{Var}(\hat e|X)=\sigma^2M_X; 6. E[\hat e_i^2|X]=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii}).

Proof. \hat\beta=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'e; take the conditional mean for 1 and the conditional variance for 2. \hat e=M_Xe gives 3. \square

3.2 Variance estimation

  • Heteroskedasticity-robust (White): \hat V(\hat\beta|X)=(X'X)^{-1}X'\operatorname{diag}[\hat e_i^2]X(X'X)^{-1}.
  • Homoskedastic: s^2=\dfrac{\hat e'\hat e}{n-k}, \hat V(\hat\beta|X)=s^2(X'X)^{-1}.
  • E[s^2]=\sigma^2 (since E[\hat e'\hat e]=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(M_X)=\sigma^2(n-k)) whereas the MLE \hat\sigma^2=\hat e'\hat e/n is biased: E[\hat\sigma^2]=\frac{n-k}n\sigma^2. The standardised residual \bar e_i=\hat e_i/\sqrt{1-h_{ii}} corrects for leverage.

3.3 The Gauss–Markov theorem

Theorem. Under A1–A4, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE): any linear unbiased estimator \tilde\beta=C'y (requiring C'X=I) has \operatorname{Var}(\tilde\beta|X)\ge\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}.

Proof. \operatorname{Var}(\tilde\beta|X)=\sigma^2C'C. Let D=C-X(X'X)^{-1}; then C'C=D'D+(X'X)^{-1} (the cross terms vanish because D'X=C'X-I=0) and D'D\ge0. \square

With heteroskedasticity (WLS / GLS): OLS is no longer BLUE; the BLUE is

\hat\beta_{W}=(X'\Sigma^{-1}X)^{-1}X'\Sigma^{-1}y,
which gives more weight to low-variance observations. Under homoskedasticity WLS = OLS.

3.4 Exact distributions under normality

Under A1–A5 (including Gaussian errors):

  1. \hat\beta|X\sim N(\beta,\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}); \hat e|X\sim N(0,\sigma^2M_X);
  2. \hat\beta and \hat e are independent (\operatorname{Cov}=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}X'M_X=0);
  3. (n-k)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-k); \hat\beta and s^2 are independent;
  4. t statistic: \hat T_j=\dfrac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j}{\sqrt{s^2[(X'X)^{-1}]_{jj}}}\sim t(n-k); likewise for linear combinations C\beta (C of size 1\times k);
  5. F statistic: for R\beta=r (R of size J\times k), \hat F=\dfrac{(R\hat\beta-r)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r)/J}{s^2}\sim F(J,n-k).

Idea of the \chi^2 proof. (n-k)s^2/\sigma^2=(e/\sigma)'M_X(e/\sigma). M_X is symmetric idempotent, so its eigenvalues are 0 or 1, with exactly n-k ones. Spectral decomposition M_X=H\Lambda H'; with z=H'(e/\sigma)\sim N(0,I) the quadratic form is \sum_{i=1}^{n-k}z_i^2. \square

Testing. For H_0:\beta_j=\beta_{0j} reject when |\hat T|>t_{\alpha/2}(n-k). The test is unbiased: if \beta_j\ne\beta_{0j} then T=T_0+\frac{\beta_j-\beta_{0j}}{\mathrm{se}} contains an extra drift, raising the rejection probability.

4. Large-Sample Theory and Tests

Intuition. In practice errors are rarely normal or homoskedastic. The saviour of large-sample theory: LLN + CLT hold for any distribution. With only E[xe]=0 and some moment conditions OLS is consistent and asymptotically normal, with the "sandwich" asymptotic variance Q^{-1}\Omega Q^{-1}, consistently estimable by White's estimator.

4.1 Consistency and asymptotic normality

Assumptions (large sample): A1 random sampling; A2 no perfect collinearity; A3′ E[x_ie_i]=0; E[x_ix_i'e_i^2]=\Omega<\infty; E[x_ix_i']=Q_{xx} finite and positive definite.

Consistency: \hat\beta=\beta+(X'X/n)^{-1}(X'e/n); by the LLN (X'X/n)^{-1}\to^pQ_{xx}^{-1} and X'e/n\to^pE[xe]=0, so \hat\beta\to^p\beta.

Asymptotic distribution: \sqrt n(\hat\beta-\beta)=(X'X/n)^{-1}\sqrt n(X'e/n) and by the CLT \sqrt n(X'e/n)\to^dN(0,\Omega), so

\sqrt n(\hat\beta-\beta)\to^dN\big(0,\ Q_{xx}^{-1}\Omega Q_{xx}^{-1}\big).
White's estimator n\hat V(\hat\beta)=(X'X/n)^{-1}\big(\frac1n\sum x_ix_i'\hat e_i^2\big)(X'X/n)^{-1}\to^pQ^{-1}\Omega Q^{-1} (expand \hat e_i=e_i-x_i'(\hat\beta-\beta); terms with \hat\beta-\beta vanish).

Under homoskedasticity this simplifies to N(0,\sigma^2Q_{xx}^{-1}) and ns^2(X'X)^{-1}\to^p\sigma^2Q_{xx}^{-1}.

Corollaries (asymptotic tests):

  • \hat T_j=\dfrac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j}{\sqrt{\hat V_{jj}}}\to^dN(0,1); likewise for linear combinations;
  • for J linear restrictions \hat F=(R\hat\beta-r)'(R\hat VR')^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r)/J\to^d\chi^2(J)/J;
  • Wald test (nonlinear restrictions g(\beta)=0): by the delta method \sqrt n(g(\hat\beta)-g(\beta))\to^dN(0,G'Q^{-1}\Omega Q^{-1}G), G=\partial g/\partial\beta, with statistic \hat W=g(\hat\beta)'(G'\hat VG)^{-1}g(\hat\beta)/J\to^d\chi^2(J)/J.

The tests are consistent: if H_1 holds, the drift \frac{\beta_j-\beta_{0j}}{\mathrm{se}} (\mathrm{se}\sim1/\sqrt n) diverges and the rejection probability tends to 1.

4.2 The sum-of-squared-residuals form of F

Theorem. With SSE_U and SSE_R the unrestricted and restricted sums of squared residuals,

\hat F=\frac{(SSE_R-SSE_U)/J}{SSE_U/(n-k)}.
Intuition: imposing a restriction raises the sum of squared residuals; reject the restriction if it rises significantly. Proof: SSE_R-SSE_U=(\tilde\beta-\hat\beta)'X'X(\tilde\beta-\hat\beta)=(R\hat\beta-r)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r). \square

4.3 Restricted estimation

Problem: \min_b(y-Xb)'(y-Xb) s.t. Rb=r. Lagrangian L=\frac12(y-Xb)'(y-Xb)-\lambda'(Rb-r) gives

\tilde\beta=\hat\beta-(X'X)^{-1}R'\big(R(X'X)^{-1}R'\big)^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r),\qquad\tilde\lambda=\big(R(X'X)^{-1}R'\big)^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r).
Properties: when the restriction is true, \tilde\beta is consistent and, under homoskedasticity, more efficient than OLS (asymptotic variance smaller by a positive semi-definite term); when it is false, \tilde\beta is inconsistent.

Special case: impose \beta_2=0 (omit X_2): \tilde\beta_1=(X_1'X_1)^{-1}X_1'y. If \beta_2\ne0, E[\tilde\beta_1|X]=\beta_1+(X_1'X_1)^{-1}X_1'X_2\beta_2 and \operatorname{plim}\tilde\beta_1=\beta_1+Q_{11}^{-1}Q_{12}\beta_2: bias (see omitted variables, Chapter 6). Trade-off: correct restrictions raise efficiency, incorrect ones bring bias — the bias–variance trade-off again.

4.4 The trinity of tests: Wald, LM, LR

The three tests answer the same question ("does R\beta=r hold?") and differ only in where they are evaluated:

Test What it looks at What must be estimated
Wald how far the unrestricted estimate is from the restriction, R\hat\beta-r unrestricted only
LM (score) whether the multiplier \tilde\lambda at the restricted estimate is significantly nonzero restricted only
LR (likelihood ratio) how much the restriction lowers the log-likelihood both

LM: \tilde\lambda=(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r), asymptotically \tilde\lambda/\sqrt n\to^dN\big(0,(RQ^{-1}R')^{-1}RQ^{-1}\Omega Q^{-1}R'(RQ^{-1}R')^{-1}\big); under homoskedasticity LM=\dfrac{(R\hat\beta-r)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r)}{\tilde s^2} with \tilde s^2 from the restricted residuals.

LR: with Gaussian homoskedastic errors, LR=2[\ln L(\hat\beta,\hat\sigma^2)-\ln L(\tilde\beta,\tilde\sigma^2)]=n\ln\dfrac{SSE_R}{SSE_U}=n\ln\Big(1+\dfrac{J}{n-k}\hat F\Big)\approx\dfrac n{n-k}\hat F (Taylor expansion).

Conclusion: the three statistics differ only through the variance estimator used (s^2,\tilde s^2,\hat\sigma^2), all consistent for \sigma^2, so the three tests are asymptotically equivalent, \to^d\chi^2(J). In the linear regression W\ge LR\ge LM often holds in order, but the differences vanish as n grows.

Confidence interval: for g(\theta), (L,U) with P(g(\theta)\in(L,U))=1-\alpha; e.g. \hat\beta_j\pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_j).

5. Specification and Practical Issues

Intuition. "Linear" means linear in parameters, not in variables. So squares, interactions and dummies can all be estimated by OLS. This chapter shows how to express nonlinearity and group differences with them, and how to test your specification and handle heteroskedasticity and collinearity.

5.1 Functional form

  • Higher-order terms: y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3+\epsilon. The marginal effect \beta_1+2\beta_2x+\cdots varies with x.
  • Interactions: y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_3x_1x_2+\epsilon; the effect of x_1 is \beta_1+\beta_3x_2.
  • Dummies: use a 0/1 variable as an ordinary regressor; a categorical variable taking values 0,1,\dots,K becomes K dummies, leaving one baseline category out (otherwise perfect collinearity with the constant — the "dummy variable trap").
  • Difference in differences: y=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{treat}+\beta_2\text{post}+\beta_3\text{treat}\times\text{post}+\epsilon.

DiD intuition: the treated group's change after the policy = common trend + policy effect. Use the control group's change to estimate the "common trend" (parallel-trends assumption); the difference of the two changes is the policy effect \hat\beta_3.

5.2 Testing the functional form: RESET

First regress y=x\beta+\epsilon to get \hat y, then regress y=x\gamma_1+\hat y^2\gamma_2+\hat y^3\gamma_3+\hat y^4\gamma_4+\mu and do an F test of H_0:\gamma_2=\gamma_3=\gamma_4=0. Intuition: if the linear specification is right, higher powers of the fitted values should have no additional explanatory power.

5.3 Heteroskedasticity: testing and efficient estimation

  • Test (Breusch–Pagan type): regress \hat e^2=\gamma_0+x'\gamma_1+\mu and do an F test of H_0:\gamma_1=0.

  • Feasible WLS:

    1. OLS to get \hat e;
    2. regress \ln\hat e^2 on x to get fitted values \hat g_i;
    3. estimate \hat\sigma_i^2=e^{\hat g_i};
    4. WLS with weights 1/\hat\sigma_i^2.

    More commonly one keeps OLS but uses White-robust standard errors (no need to know the form of heteroskedasticity).

5.4 Prediction and multicollinearity

  • Prediction: for a new observation x_i, \hat y_i=x_i'\hat\beta with forecast-error variance \operatorname{AVar}(\hat y_i-y_i|X)=x_i'\operatorname{AVar}(\hat\beta)x_i+\operatorname{Var}(e_i|x_i): parameter uncertainty plus irreducible noise (under homoskedasticity the latter is \sigma^2).
  • Multicollinearity: in the partitioned model y=x_1'\beta_1+x_K\beta_K+\epsilon, under homoskedasticity
    \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_K|X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{(1-R_K^2)\,x_K'M_\iota x_K},
    where R_K^2 is the R^2 from regressing x_K on the other regressors. \frac1{1-R_K^2} is the variance inflation factor (VIF). Meaning: when a regressor is well predicted by the others its coefficient is imprecisely estimated (large standard error) — but the estimator remains unbiased and consistent, merely imprecise; only perfect collinearity makes estimation impossible.

6. Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables and GMM

Intuition. OLS is consistent because E[xe]=0. If a regressor is correlated with the error — endogeneity — OLS estimates the "wrong thing" and no sample size fixes it. Endogeneity has three main sources: omitted variables, measurement error, simultaneity. The idea of an instrumental variable (IV): find an exogenous source of variation z that affects y only through x and use the part of x's variation driven by z to identify the effect.

6.1 Sources of endogeneity

(a) Omitted variables. The true model is y=X_1\beta_1+X_2\beta_2+e but we regress y on X_1 only. If X_2=X_1\delta+\mu,

\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+(X_1'X_1)^{-1}X_1'X_2\beta_2+(X_1'X_1)^{-1}X_1'e\ \Rightarrow\ \operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\delta\beta_2.
Bias = (effect of the omitted variable on y, \beta_2) × (its correlation with X_1, \delta). In small samples E[\hat\beta_1|X_1]=\beta_1+\delta\beta_2 (biased), in large samples it is inconsistent. Example: regressing wages on schooling while omitting "ability": ability correlates positively with both, so the schooling coefficient is overstated.

(b) Measurement error (errors in variables). We observe only S=X+u (u independent of X,e). Then \hat\beta\to^p\beta\cdot\dfrac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_u^2}: attenuation toward zero. Intuition: noise makes x look highly variable without explaining y, so the slope is "diluted". The ratio \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_u^2} is the reliability ratio.

(c) Simultaneity. Supply Q=\beta_1P+e_1 and demand Q=\beta_2P+e_2 jointly determine (P,Q). The observed (P,Q) is an equilibrium affected by both supply and demand shocks, so P is correlated with both e_1 and e_2; regressing Q on P yields some mixture of the two curves and neither can be identified.

6.2 Instrumental variables

Setup: y=X_1\beta_1+X_2\beta_2+e with E[e|X_2]\ne0 (X_2 endogenous, k-dimensional). Find Z (J-dimensional) with

  • exogeneity (exclusion): E[Ze]=0 (Z affects y only through X_2);
  • relevance: E[ZX_2'] has full rank.

First stage and reduced form: X_2=X_1\Gamma_1+Z\Gamma_2+u; substituting, y=X_1\gamma_1+Z\gamma_2+v with \gamma_2=\Gamma_2\beta_2.

Identification:

  • Order condition: J\ge k (at least as many instruments as endogenous variables);
  • Rank condition: \operatorname{rank}(\Gamma_2)=k (the first-stage coefficient matrix has full rank).

IV estimator (J=k): \hat\beta^{IV}=\hat\Gamma_2^{-1}\hat\gamma_2=(Z'X)^{-1}Z'y. Scalar case (Wald estimator): \hat\beta^{IV}=\dfrac{\operatorname{cov}(y,z)}{\operatorname{cov}(x,z)} — the instrument's effect on y divided by its effect on x.

Intuition: z moves x by \operatorname{cov}(x,z) and y by \operatorname{cov}(y,z); since z affects y only through x, the ratio is the effect of x on y.

6.3 Generalised method of moments (GMM)

Moment conditions: E[z_i(y_i-x_i'\beta)]=0, where z_i contains exogenous regressors and instruments. When J>k (more moments than parameters) the sample moments cannot all be zero, so minimise a weighted distance:

\bar\beta=\arg\min_\beta\ (y-X\beta)'ZW_nZ'(y-X\beta)\ \Rightarrow\ \bar\beta=(X'ZW_nZ'X)^{-1}X'ZW_nZ'y.

Assumptions: W_n\to W symmetric positive definite; E[z_ie_i]=0; Q_{zx}=E[z_ix_i'] exists; \Omega=E[z_iz_i'e_i^2]<\infty.

Asymptotics:

\sqrt n(\bar\beta-\beta)\to^dN\big(0,\ (Q_{zx}'WQ_{zx})^{-1}Q_{zx}'W\Omega WQ_{zx}(Q_{zx}'WQ_{zx})^{-1}\big),
where Q_{zx},\Omega are consistently estimated by Z'X/n and \frac1n\sum\hat e_i^2z_iz_i'.

Optimal weight: for any W the variance above is \ge(Q_{zx}'\Omega^{-1}Q_{zx})^{-1}, with equality at W=\Omega^{-1}. Proof: the difference is Q'\Omega^{-1}Q-(Q'WQ)(Q'W\Omega WQ)^{-1}(Q'WQ)=A'M_BA\ge0 (a "regression sum of squares", hence positive semi-definite), with A=\Omega^{-1/2}Q, B=\Omega^{1/2}WQ. \square Feasible efficient GMM: first estimate with any W to get \hat e, estimate \hat\Omega, then set W_n=\hat\Omega^{-1}.

J=k (just identified): \bar\beta=(Z'X)^{-1}Z'y, independent of the weight.

6.4 Two-stage least squares (2SLS)

\hat\beta^{2SLS}=\big(X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X\big)^{-1}X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'y=(X'P_ZX)^{-1}X'P_Zy.

The two stages: first regress X on Z to get \hat X=P_ZX (the "clean" part of X explained by the instruments); then regress y on \hat X. 2SLS is GMM with weight W_n=(Z'Z/n)^{-1}, optimal under homoskedasticity (E[z_iz_i'e_i^2]=\sigma^2E[z_iz_i']).

Warning: running the two stages by hand gives the right coefficients but wrong second-stage standard errors (they use \hat X instead of X to form residuals); use a proper 2SLS command.

6.5 Weak instruments and specification tests

  • Weak instruments: the rank condition "almost" fails, \Gamma_2=\delta/\sqrt n\to0. IV/GMM is then inconsistent and its finite-sample distribution is far from normal (large bias). Test: in the first stage X_2=X_1\Gamma_1+Z\Gamma_2+u test H_0:\Gamma_2=0 (F or Wald); rule of thumb: first-stage F>10.
  • Over-identification and Hansen's J test: when J>k we can test whether the instruments are all exogenous:
    \hat J=n\,(y-X\bar\beta)'Z\hat\Omega^{-1}Z'(y-X\bar\beta)\to^d\chi^2(J-k),\qquad H_0:E[z_ie_i]=0.
    Intuition: if all moment conditions are valid, estimates from any subset should agree; J measures how much they "fight". Rejection means at least one instrument is invalid (but not which). Proof idea (homoskedasticity/2SLS): J=\hat e'P_Z\hat e can be written as a quadratic form e'B(I-B(B'B)^{-1}B')Be, asymptotically a sum of J-k squared standard normals.
  • Hausman test (testing endogeneity): compare OLS and IV: H=n(\hat\beta-\bar\beta)'V^+(\hat\beta-\bar\beta)\to^d\chi^2(k), V=V(\bar\beta)-V(\hat\beta). Intuition: if x is exogenous OLS is consistent and more efficient so the two should be close; a big difference signals endogeneity. Regression form (control function): regress X_2 on (X_1,Z) to get the residual \hat u, then regress y=X_1\beta_1+X_2\beta_2+\hat u\rho+\epsilon and test H_0:\rho=0 with an F test; the coefficient on X_2 in this regression is exactly the 2SLS estimate.

7. M-Estimation and Discrete Choice

Intuition. Many estimators "maximise a sample objective": OLS (minimise squares), MLE (maximise log-likelihood), GMM. M-estimation provides a unified large-sample theory: if the population objective has a unique maximiser and the sample objective converges to it uniformly, the sample maximiser is consistent; then a Taylor expansion of the first-order condition gives asymptotic normality. Discrete-choice models (probit, logit) are its most important application.

7.1 Consistency of M-estimators

Setup: population objective Q(\theta), sample objective Q_N(\theta), \theta_0=\arg\max Q(\theta), \hat\theta_N=\arg\max Q_N(\theta).

Assumptions (Newey–McFadden): ①Q(\theta) has a unique maximiser \theta_0; ②the parameter space \Theta is compact; ③Q(\theta) is continuous; ④Q_N(\theta)\to^pQ(\theta) uniformly on \Theta.

Theorem (consistency). \hat\theta_N\to^p\theta_0.

Proof idea. Take any neighbourhood \mathcal N of \theta_0. (1) Since \hat\theta_N maximises Q_N and convergence is uniform, Q(\hat\theta_N)>Q_N(\hat\theta_N)-\frac\epsilon3\ge Q_N(\theta_0)-\frac\epsilon3>Q(\theta_0)-\epsilon with probability tending to 1. (2) \Theta\setminus\mathcal N is compact and Q continuous, so the maximum Q(\theta^*) over it is <Q(\theta_0) (uniqueness). With \epsilon=Q(\theta_0)-Q(\theta^*), Q(\hat\theta_N)>Q(\theta^*) with probability tending to 1, so \hat\theta_N\in\mathcal N. \square

Corollary (MLE consistency): iid with density f(z|\theta), \theta\in\Theta compact, identified (\theta\ne\theta_0\Rightarrow f(\cdot|\theta)\ne f(\cdot|\theta_0)), \ln f continuous, E[\sup_\theta|\ln f|]<\infty. Then \hat\theta\to^p\theta_0.

7.2 Asymptotic distribution

Assumptions: \theta_0 is interior; Q_N twice continuously differentiable; \sqrt N\nabla_\theta Q_N(\theta_0)\to^dN(0,\Sigma); \sup_\theta\|\nabla_{\theta\theta}Q_N-H\|\to^p0; H invertible.

Theorem. \sqrt N(\hat\theta_N-\theta_0)\to^dN(0,H^{-1}\Sigma H^{-1}).

Proof. The first-order condition is \nabla_\theta Q_N(\hat\theta_N)=0. Taylor-expand around \theta_0: 0=\nabla Q_N(\theta_0)+\nabla^2Q_N(\tilde\theta_N)(\hat\theta_N-\theta_0), so \sqrt N(\hat\theta_N-\theta_0)=-[\nabla^2Q_N(\tilde\theta)]^{-1}\sqrt N\nabla Q_N(\theta_0)\to^dN(0,H^{-1}\Sigma H^{-1}). \square

MLE: here the information-matrix equality \Sigma=-H=J holds (variance of the score = minus the expected Hessian), so \sqrt N(\hat\theta-\theta_0)\to^dN(0,J^{-1}), J=E[\nabla\ln f\,(\nabla\ln f)']. (Cramér–Rao bound: the MLE is asymptotically efficient.)

7.3 Binary choice: the linear index model

Latent variable. y^*=X\beta+\epsilon, observed y=\mathbb 1\{y^*\ge0\}; \epsilon independent of X with CDF G continuous and symmetric about 0. Then

P(y=1|X)=P(\epsilon\ge-X\beta)=G(X\beta).

Model G(z) Feature
Linear probability model (LPM) z simple, but predicted probabilities leave [0,1]
Probit \Phi(z) normal errors
Logit \dfrac{e^z}{1+e^z} logistic errors; coefficients are slopes of the log-odds

Marginal effects: \dfrac{\partial P(y=1|X)}{\partial x_j}=\beta_jg(X\beta), g=G'. LPM: \beta_j; Probit: \beta_j\phi(X\beta); Logit: \beta_jG(X\beta)(1-G(X\beta)). They vary with X, so say where you report them:

  • at an interesting X;
  • PEA (Partial Effect at the Average): at the sample mean \bar X;
  • APE (Average Partial Effect): average of the marginal effect over everyone in the sample. (Usually preferred.)

7.4 Conditional maximum likelihood

The joint likelihood is l(y,X|\theta)=l(y|X,\theta)\,l(X): if l(X) does not involve \theta, maximise the conditional log-likelihood:

Q_N(\beta)=\frac1N\sum_i\big[y_i\ln G(X_i\beta)+(1-y_i)\ln(1-G(X_i\beta))\big].
By M-estimation theory, under identification, compact parameter space, continuity of \ln G and a dominance condition, CMLE is consistent and
\sqrt N(\hat\beta-\beta)\to^dN(0,J^{-1}),\qquad J=E\Big[\frac{g(x\beta)^2}{G(x\beta)[1-G(x\beta)]}xx'\Big].
(Probit and Logit have no closed form; solve iteratively by Newton's method.)

7.5 Multiple choice

Multinomial logit: y\in\{0,1,\dots,J\}, P(y=j|X)=\dfrac{\exp(X\beta_j)}{\sum_{h=0}^J\exp(X\beta_h)}, normalising \beta_0=0. Conditional logit (McFadden): each alternative has its own attributes x_{ij}, y^*_{ij}=x_{ij}\beta+e_{ij}, with e_{ij} iid type-I extreme value F(e)=\exp(-e^{-e}), giving

P(y_i=j|X_i)=\frac{\exp(x_{ij}\beta)}{\sum_{h=0}^J\exp(x_{ih}\beta)}.
Multinomial logit is a special case (set x_{ij}=(d_{0j}X_i,\dots,d_{Jj}X_i)). Beware IIA (independence of irrelevant alternatives): the odds ratio between any two alternatives does not depend on the others — sometimes unrealistic (the "red bus / blue bus" problem).

Ordered response: y\in\{1,\dots,J\} naturally ordered, y^*=x\beta+e, y=j\iff y^*\in[\alpha_{j-1},\alpha_j), so

P(y=j|x)=G(\alpha_j-x\beta)-G(\alpha_{j-1}-x\beta).

8. Bootstrap, Clustering, Quantile Regression and Censoring

8.1 The bootstrap

Intuition. We want the sampling distribution of an estimator but have one sample. Bootstrap: treat the sample as a stand-in for the population, resample it with replacement, recompute the estimator each time, and use the resulting distribution to approximate the true sampling distribution. It is especially useful for complicated estimators with no analytic standard error.

Algorithm: ①compute \hat\theta=h(X_1,\dots,X_n) from the original sample; ②draw n observations with replacement and compute \hat\theta^1; ③repeat B times to get \hat\theta^1,\dots,\hat\theta^B; ④use their distribution for standard errors, confidence intervals or tests. Theory: as the number of repetitions grows the bootstrap distribution converges to the estimator's true distribution (under regularity conditions).

8.2 Clustering

Intuition. People in the same village or school share shocks, so errors are correlated within groups. The independence assumption fails and OLS standard errors are too small. Cluster-robust standard errors allow arbitrary within-group correlation provided different groups are independent.

Model: y_g=X_g\beta+u_g, g=1,\dots,G; y_g,u_g are N_g\times1 and X_g is N_g\times K. OLS is unchanged: \hat\beta=(\sum X_g'X_g)^{-1}\sum X_g'y_g.

Variance: V(\hat\beta|X)=(X'X)^{-1}X'\Omega X(X'X)^{-1} with block-diagonal \Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\Omega_1,\dots,\Omega_G). Estimator:

\hat V=(X'X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{g=1}^GX_g'\hat u_g\hat u_g'X_g\Big)(X'X)^{-1}.
Assumptions: conditional exogeneity E[u_g|X]=0; groups iid; \sum E[X_g'X_g] invertible; E[X_g'\Omega_gX_g]=\Sigma. Then OLS is unbiased, consistent as G\to\infty and \sqrt G(\hat\beta-\beta)\to^dN(0,Q^{-1}\Sigma Q^{-1}).

Cautions: ①the asymptotics require the number of groups G\to\infty; with few groups (say G<30) they are unreliable, and Stata applies the finite-sample correction c=\frac G{G-1}\frac{N-1}{N-K}; ②clustering handles heteroskedasticity too, so no extra robust correction is needed; ③data can be clustered along several dimensions (multiway clustering), which noticeably reduces precision.

8.3 Quantile regression

Intuition. OLS estimates the conditional mean; if you care about a position in the distribution (the median, the 10th percentile of low earners) the mean is not enough. Quantile regression estimates the conditional quantile Q_\alpha(y|x)=x'\beta_\alpha.

Quantile: P(y<Q_\alpha)=\alpha. Check (linear) loss function:

L_\alpha(y,\theta)=\begin{cases}\alpha\,|y-\theta|,&y\ge\theta\\(1-\alpha)\,|y-\theta|,&y<\theta\end{cases}
The \theta minimising E[L_\alpha(y,\theta)] is exactly the \alpha-quantile (squared loss gives the mean, absolute loss the median).

8.4 Censoring (top coding)

Setup: y^*=X\beta+\epsilon and we observe y=y^* if y^*\le c and y=c if y^*>c (e.g. incomes above a threshold are recorded as "top bracket"). Plain OLS is biased. Robustness of quantile regression: for y^*\le c the CDF of y equals that of y^*, so quantiles below the censoring point are still estimated correctly; above it we only obtain a lower bound on the CDF, P(y\le c|x)\le P(y^*\le c|x) — partial identification.

9. Panel Data

Intuition. Panel data follow the same individuals over several periods. Their charm: individuals have many time-invariant but unobserved traits (ability, culture, geography). If these correlate with the regressors, ordinary OLS suffers omitted-variable bias; but a panel can difference them away using within-individual variation (comparing an individual with herself over time).

9.1 The panel model and pooled OLS

y_{it}=x_{it}\beta+c_i+u_{it},\qquad i=1,\dots,N,\ t=1,\dots,T\ (N\to\infty,\ T\text{ fixed}).

c_i is the individual effect (unobserved, time-invariant) and u_{it} the idiosyncratic error. Pooled OLS treats c_i+u_{it} as the error and needs E[x_{it}'(c_i+u_{it})]=0 — i.e. c_i uncorrelated with x_{it}.

9.2 The fixed-effects (FE) estimator

Within transformation: \bar y_i=\bar x_i\beta+c_i+\bar u_i; subtracting removes c_i:

\ddot y_{it}=\ddot x_{it}\beta+\ddot u_{it},\qquad\ddot y_{it}=y_{it}-\bar y_i.
\hat\beta_{FE}=\Big(\sum_i\sum_t\ddot x_{it}'\ddot x_{it}\Big)^{-1}\sum_i\sum_t\ddot x_{it}'\ddot y_{it}.

Assumptions: ①strict exogeneity E[u_{it}|x_i,c_i]=0 (all t); ②rank condition \operatorname{rank}E[\ddot X_i'\ddot X_i]=K; ③no serial correlation / homoskedasticity E[u_iu_i'|x_i,c_i]=\sigma_u^2I_T. Results: under ①② FE is consistent; under ①–③ \sqrt N(\hat\beta_{FE}-\beta)\to^dN(0,\sigma_u^2E[\ddot X_i'\ddot X_i]^{-1}) and \hat\sigma_u^2=\dfrac{\sum\hat u_{it}^2}{N(T-1)-K}\to^p\sigma_u^2 (degrees of freedom subtract the N estimated means).

Price: time-invariant variables (sex, nationality) are eliminated by demeaning, so their coefficients cannot be estimated.

Dummy-variable regression (LSDV): include a dummy per individual. \hat\beta_{DV}=\hat\beta_{FE} and \hat c_i=\bar y_i-\bar x_i\hat\beta_{FE} is unbiased but inconsistent (T fixed, so each c_i is estimated from only T observations).

9.3 Serial correlation and robust inference

If errors are correlated over time the homoskedastic formula fails. Test: regress \hat u_{it} on \hat u_{i,t-1}; under H_0 (u_{it} serially uncorrelated) the coefficient is \delta=-\dfrac1{T-1} (demeaning itself introduces negative correlation: \operatorname{corr}(\ddot u_{it},\ddot u_{i,t-1})=-\frac1{T-1}). Robust (cluster) variance:

\widehat{\operatorname{AVar}}(\hat\beta_{FE})=\Big(\sum\ddot X_i'\ddot X_i\Big)^{-1}\Big(\sum\ddot X_i'\hat u_i\hat u_i'\ddot X_i\Big)\Big(\sum\ddot X_i'\ddot X_i\Big)^{-1}
(i.e. cluster by individual). FEGLS: drop one period (to avoid singularity), estimate \Omega=E[\ddot u_i\ddot u_i'] (size (T-1)\times(T-1)) and run GLS for a more efficient estimator.

9.4 The first-difference (FD) estimator

Differencing removes c_i: \Delta y_{it}=\Delta x_{it}\beta+\Delta u_{it}, \hat\beta_{FD}=(\sum\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i)^{-1}\sum\Delta X_i'\Delta y_i. Assumptions as for FE but homoskedasticity becomes E[\Delta u_i\Delta u_i'|x_i,c_i]=\sigma_e^2I_{T-1}. Serial-correlation test: regress \hat e_{it} on \hat e_{i,t-1}; under H_0, \delta=-\frac12 (the differenced errors \Delta u_{it} and \Delta u_{i,t-1} share u_{i,t-1}: \operatorname{cov}=-\sigma_u^2, \operatorname{var}=2\sigma_u^2).

FE versus FD: if u_{it} has no serial correlation, FE is most efficient; if u_{it} is a random walk (\Delta u_{it} serially uncorrelated), FD is most efficient. With T=2 they coincide.

9.5 Random effects (RE)

Assumption: c_i is uncorrelated with x_{it}, E[c_i|x_i]=0. Then v_{it}=c_i+u_{it} has covariance structure \Omega=\sigma_u^2I_T+\sigma_c^2\iota_T\iota_T' and we use feasible GLS:

\hat\beta_{RE}=\Big(\sum X_i'\hat\Omega^{-1}X_i\Big)^{-1}\sum X_i'\hat\Omega^{-1}y_i,
with \hat\Omega estimated from pooled-OLS residuals. RE is more efficient than FE (and can estimate time-invariant variables), but needs the stronger assumption c_i\perp x_{it}. Choose between FE and RE with a Hausman test: if c_i correlates with x, RE is inconsistent.

9.6 Endogeneity in panels

  • FEIV: if \operatorname{cov}(\ddot x_{it},\ddot z_{it})\ne0 and E[u_{it}|z_i,c_i]=0 (all t), run IV on demeaned data;
  • FDIV: run IV on differenced data, requiring only E[u_{it}|w_{is},c_i]=0 for s<t (sequential exogeneity).
  • Sequential exogeneity E[u_{it}|x_{is},c_i]=0 (only for s\le t, not future x): then FE and FD are both inconsistent (but FE's bias shrinks as T\to\infty, so it is preferable); one can use lags of x_{is} (s<t) as instruments in FDIV, but not FEIV (which needs strictly exogenous instruments).
  • Clustering with fixed effects: y_{jg}=x_{jg}\beta+v_g+\epsilon_{jg}. The fixed effect v_g has absorbed the variation shared within the group; clustering must consider errors that are still shared within the group beyond the fixed effect.

10. Counterfactuals and Selection

Intuition. Causal questions are counterfactual: "what would this person's wage have been had she not gone to college?" But each person is observed in only one state. This is a missing-data problem. Without assumptions we can only bound the outcome (partial identification); each added assumption shrinks the bounds. This "add assumptions gradually, shrink the range gradually" approach is more honest than assuming "linear and exogenous" from the start.

10.1 Missing data and partial identification

Setup: data of the form (x,z,yz) with z=1 if y is observed. Goal: P(y\le t|X=x). By total probability

P(y\le t|x)=P(y\le t|x,z=1)P(z=1|x)+P(y\le t|x,z=0)P(z=0|x).
We know only that the unobserved second term lies in [0,1], giving the partial-identification interval
P(y\le t|x)\in\big[P(y\le t|x,z=1)P(z=1|x),\ P(y\le t|x,z=1)P(z=1|x)+P(z=0|x)\big].
Its width is exactly the missing fraction P(z=0|x): the more data are missing, the more uncertainty.

Missing at random (MAR): P(y\le t|x,z=1)=P(y\le t|x,z=0) (missingness unrelated to the outcome). The interval collapses to the point P(y\le t|x,z=1) and OLS on the observed data alone remains unbiased and consistent.

10.2 The Rubin–Neyman causal model

Potential outcomes: a treatment set \mathcal T; individual j's outcome under treatment t is y_j(t); the actual treatment is z_j and we observe y_j=y_j(z_j). The goal is D[y_j(t')-y_j(t)] (D a functional such as the expectation). The problem: for t\ne z_j, y_j(t) is never observed — causal inference is a missing-data problem.

Partial identification: P(y_j(d)\le t|x)\in\big[P(y_j\le t|x,z=d)P(z=d|x),\ P(y_j\le t|x,z=d)P(z=d|x)+P(z\ne d|x)\big]. For functionals that respect first-order stochastic dominance (such as the expectation) the bounds on E[y(t)-y(s)] depend on bounds y_0,y_1 of the outcome.

Adding assumptions step by step:

  1. Random assignment: P(y(d)\le t|x,z)=P(y(d)\le t|x). Then E[y(0)|z=1]=E[y(0)|z=0], E[y(1)|z=0]=E[y(1)|z=1]: counterfactuals are identified from the control/treated groups (point identification).
  2. Treatment choice by optimisation (Manski): people choose the treatment best for themselves, y_j(d)\le_{FOSD}y_j(z_j). Binary case: E[y(0)|z=1]\le E[y(1)|z=1], E[y(1)|z=0]\le E[y(0)|z=0] (each person's chosen treatment is better for her).
  3. Monotone treatment response (MTR): if treatments are ordered, t\ge s\Rightarrow y_j(t)\ge_{FOSD}y_j(s) (treatment never hurts, e.g. more schooling does not lower earnings potential).
  4. Monotone treatment selection (MTS): s'\ge s\Rightarrow E[y(t)|z=s']\ge E[y(t)|z=s] (those choosing more treatment would have done better anyway, e.g. "high-ability people get more education").
  5. Further structural assumptions (e.g. y(\cdot) concave) shrink the interval more.

MTR and MTS are different assumptions. In y=X\beta+e, MTR is \beta\ge0 (treatment has no negative effect), MTS is E[e|z=s']\ge E[e|z=s] (selection is positively related to the error).

10.3 Selection models

The problem. Regress \ln w=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{educ}+u but wages are observed only for those who work; non-workers' potential wages are unseen. This is sample selection: the observed sample is not random.

Homogeneous reservation wage (identification): a person works iff wage y\ge R(x) (the reservation wage, same for equal x). Let y^*(x)=\min_iy_i(x). For t\ge R(x), non-workers' wages are necessarily <t, so P(y\le t|x,z=0)=1 and P(y\le t|x)=P(y\le t|x,z=1)P(z=1|x)+P(z=0|x) is point-identified — quantiles above the reservation wage have no missing-data problem.

Heckman two-step. Let \ln y=x\beta_1+\epsilon_1, \ln R=x\beta_2+\epsilon_2, (\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\sim N(0,\Sigma) independent of x. The wage is observed iff \ln y>\ln R (z=1).

Step 1 (selection equation, Probit): P(z=1|x)=\Phi\big(x\tilde\beta\big), \tilde\beta=\dfrac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{\sigma}, \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_2-\epsilon_1). Estimate \hat{\tilde\beta} by Probit.

Step 2 (outcome equation with a correction term): in the selected sample

E[\ln y|x,z=1]=x\beta_1+\sigma_{1u}\,m(x\tilde\beta),\qquad m(s)=\frac{\phi(s)}{\Phi(s)},
where m is the inverse Mills ratio and \sigma_{1u}=\operatorname{cov}\big(\epsilon_1,\tfrac{\epsilon_2-\epsilon_1}{\sigma}\big). So regress \ln y on x and m(x\hat{\tilde\beta}) in the selected sample; omitting m causes omitted-variable bias.

Intuition: selection lets us see only people with low reservation wages or high wages; those selected are no longer random on unobservables. The inverse Mills ratio measures "how strongly selected" a person is, and putting it in the regression controls for that non-randomness.

11. Treatment Effects

Intuition. Chapter 10 asked "what can we know with no assumptions?". This chapter takes the other road: use structural designs (instruments, discontinuities, conditional unconfoundedness) to point-identify the causal effect for a certain group. An important reminder: different methods identify effects for different populations — do not conflate them.

11.1 Local average treatment effects (LATE)

Setup: binary treatment x, binary instrument z (exogenous, unrelated to the error). The IV (Wald) estimator is

\hat\beta_{IV}=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(y,z)}{\operatorname{cov}(x,z)}=\frac{E[y|z=1]-E[y|z=0]}{E[x|z=1]-E[x|z=0]}.
Four types (by response x(z) to the instrument):

Type x(0),x(1) Share
Never-taker 0,0 \pi_n
Complier 0,1 \pi_c
Defier 1,0 \pi_d
Always-taker 1,1 \pi_a

Monotonicity: x_j(1)\ge x_j(0) (no defiers, \pi_d=0).

Derivation.

  • Denominator: E[x|z=0]=\pi_a, E[x|z=1]=\pi_a+\pi_c, so E[x|z=1]-E[x|z=0]=\pi_c.
  • Numerator: E[y|z=1]=E[y(1)|C]\pi_c+E[y(0)|N]\pi_n+E[y(1)|A]\pi_a; E[y|z=0]=E[y(0)|C]\pi_c+E[y(0)|N]\pi_n+E[y(1)|A]\pi_a. The never- and always-taker terms are the same in both and cancel: E[y|z=1]-E[y|z=0]=E[y(1)-y(0)|C]\,\pi_c.

Hence

\boxed{\ \hat\beta_{IV}=E[y(1)-y(0)\mid\text{complier}]\ }.

Key point: IV estimates the average treatment effect for compliers (LATE), not for everyone (ATE). Compliers may be a small share, and we cannot tell who they are. To get the ATE we would also need E[y(0)|A] and E[y(1)|N], which are impossible without further assumptions.

11.2 Regression discontinuity (RD)

Intuition. Many policies are assigned by a cutoff: pass if the score is \ge60, receive a pension at age \ge65. People just either side of the cutoff are almost identical yet get different treatment — a "quasi-natural experiment". Comparing outcomes across the cutoff gives the causal effect of treatment.

Setup: a running variable z, treatment x=\mathbb 1\{z\ge c\}.

Sharp RD. The causal effect at c is

E[y(1)-y(0)\mid z=c]=\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}E[y|z=c+\epsilon]-\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}E[y|z=c-\epsilon],
provided E[y(d)|z] is continuous at c (nothing else jumps at c).

Fuzzy RD. The treatment probability jumps at c but not from 0 to 1: \lim P(x=1|z=c^+)\ne\lim P(x=1|z=c^-). The estimator is the ratio of jumps

\frac{\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}E[y|z=c+\epsilon]-\lim E[y|z=c-\epsilon]}{\lim E[x|z=c+\epsilon]-\lim E[x|z=c-\epsilon]}=E[y(1)-y(0)\mid z=c,\text{ complier}]\ (\text{LATE}).
(This is IV using "being above the cutoff" as the instrument; in sharp RD everyone is a complier.)

Implementation.

  • Local linear regression: fit a line on each side of the cutoff,
    y_i=\alpha_L+\beta_L(z_i-c)+e\ (z_i<c),\qquad y_i=\alpha_H+\beta_H(z_i-c)+e\ (z_i>c).
    The sharp RD estimator is \hat\alpha_H-\hat\alpha_L; the fuzzy version runs the same local regressions for the treatment indicator x giving \hat\gamma_H-\hat\gamma_L, and the estimator is \dfrac{\hat\alpha_H-\hat\alpha_L}{\hat\gamma_H-\hat\gamma_L}.
  • McCrary test: the density of the running variable should show no jump at c (otherwise people can manipulate their score to cross it and comparability is destroyed).

11.3 Exogenously assigned treatment: matching and propensity scores

Assumptions:

  • Conditional unconfoundedness: (y(1),y(0))\perp z\mid x (given x, who gets treated is "as good as random");
  • Overlap: 0<P(z=1|x)<1 (for every x there are both treated and controls).

Then ATE=E\big[E[y|x,z=1]-E[y|x,z=0]\big]=\sum_xP(x)\big(E[y|x,z=1]-E[y|x,z=0]\big). The key is to estimate the conditional means E[y|x,z].

Kernel regression (nonparametric). Estimate E[y|x=c] without assuming a functional form:

  • discrete x: \hat\mu(c)=\dfrac{\sum y_i\mathbb 1[x_i=c]}{\sum\mathbb 1[x_i=c]} (subsample mean);
  • continuous x: \hat\mu(c)=\dfrac{\sum y_iK\big(\frac{x_i-c}{h}\big)}{\sum K\big(\frac{x_i-c}{h}\big)}, where K is a kernel (maximal at 0, decreasing away from it, tending to 0) and h the bandwidth. Observations closer to c get more weight; small h ⟹ small bias, large variance, and vice versa (bias–variance trade-off).

Matching estimator. For each person i find the m people in the other group with the most similar x, L_m(i), and use their average outcome to fill in the missing counterfactual:

\hat y_i(z)=\begin{cases}y_i&z_i=z\\\frac1m\sum_{j\in L_m(i)}y_j&z_i\ne z\end{cases},\qquad\widehat{ATE}=\frac1N\sum_i\big[\hat y_i(1)-\hat y_i(0)\big].

Propensity score. e(x)=P(z=1|x). Theorem (inverse-probability weighting): under unconfoundedness

E[y(1)]=E\Big[\frac{zy}{e(x)}\Big],\qquad E[y(0)]=E\Big[\frac{(1-z)y}{1-e(x)}\Big].
Proof: E\big[\frac{zy}{e(x)}\big]=E\big[\frac{z\,y(1)}{e(x)}\big]=E\Big[E\big[\frac{z\,y(1)}{e(x)}\big|x\big]\Big]=E\Big[\frac{e(x)E[y(1)|x]}{e(x)}\Big]=E[y(1)] (unconfoundedness gives E[zy(1)|x]=e(x)E[y(1)|x]). \square

Intuition: among the treated, people with a low propensity score are "rare", so give them larger weight 1/e(x) so the weighted treated group "represents" everyone. The overlap assumption keeps weights finite; with propensity scores near 0 or 1 estimates become very unstable. Estimators: \hat y(1)=\frac1N\sum\frac{z_iy_i}{\hat e(x_i)}, \hat y(0)=\frac1N\sum\frac{(1-z_i)y_i}{1-\hat e(x_i)}, with \hat e typically from a logit/probit.

12. Bayesian Statistics

Intuition. The frequentist treats the parameter as an unknown constant; the data are random. The Bayesian treats the parameter as a random variable, expresses beliefs before seeing data as a prior P(\theta), updates it with the likelihood and obtains the posterior.

Bayes' formula:

P(\theta|y)=\frac{P(y|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(y)}\propto\text{likelihood}\times\text{prior}.

Example: Bernoulli / Beta (conjugate prior). y_i\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\theta) with M successes in N trials, P(y|\theta)=\theta^M(1-\theta)^{N-M}. Take the prior \theta\sim\text{Beta}(\alpha,\delta), P(\theta)\propto\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\delta-1}. Then

P(\theta|y)\propto\theta^{M+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{N-M+\delta-1}\ \Rightarrow\ \theta|y\sim\text{Beta}(\alpha+M,\ \delta+N-M).
Reading: the prior acts like "\alpha-1 successes and \delta-1 failures of pseudo-data seen beforehand"; the posterior mean \dfrac{\alpha+M}{\alpha+\delta+N} is a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample frequency, tilting toward the data as the sample grows.

Bernstein–von Mises theorem: under regularity conditions and large samples, the Bayesian posterior and the sampling distribution of the frequentist estimator approximately coincide — the influence of the prior vanishes as N\to\infty. So in large samples the two schools usually agree; differences are mainly in small samples and the subjective part of the prior.

13. Looking Back: One Thread

Problem Population moment Estimator Source of consistency Watch out for
Conditional mean E[xe]=0 OLS LLN needs no endogeneity

Ideas to take away:

  • OLS = projection: residuals are orthogonal to regressors; FWL shows that "controlling" means removing the common part.
  • Finite sample (normal) → large sample (any distribution): with LLN + CLT + the delta method, asymptotic variances are all sandwiches A^{-1}BA^{-1}.
  • Sources of endogeneity: omitted variables (\delta\beta_2), measurement error (attenuation), simultaneity; IV identifies from variation that works "only through x".
  • The testing trinity: Wald, LM, LR are asymptotically equivalent; they differ in "where to evaluate".
  • Identification matters more than estimation: without credible identification even beautiful standard errors cannot answer a causal question.
  • Different methods identify effects for different populations: IV/RD give a LATE, matching/IPW give an ATE, and each relies on its own assumptions.
